observation_kind: 120 distinct official-source checks plus 12 exact-data/runtime blockers; each applied once to 3 preserved candidates; no validation-mode multiplication.
f: Ordnance Survey is the national mapping agency of Great Britain.
Ordnance Survey mapping records topographic features that existed when the survey was made.
Ordnance Survey map detail is not intended to represent legal property boundaries.
Historically HM Land Registry plans were based on large-scale Ordnance Survey paper mapping.
HM Land Registry now uses OS MasterMap as the base for its plans.
OS MasterMap is described as Ordnance Survey's definitive large-scale digital map product.
Ordnance Survey colours are suppressed on HM Land Registry-produced plans so registry colour references remain clear.
OS MasterMap is supplied and maintained in a seamless and consistent form.
OS MasterMap is surveyed and produced at different scales.
HM Land Registry title plans for urban land are broadly prepared at 1:1250.
HM Land Registry title plans for rural land are broadly prepared at 1:2500.
HM Land Registry title plans for mountain and moorland are broadly prepared at 1:10000.
Standard surveying and mapping cannot reproduce the exact ground position of every physical feature.
The difference between mapped and real-world feature positions is described as specified accuracy tolerance.
Distances scaled from OS mapping may differ from ground measurements.
Mapping accuracy varies with map scale and the original survey method.
A line on 1:1250 mapping roughly represents 0.3 metres on the ground.
A line on 1:2500 mapping roughly represents 0.6 metres on the ground.
HM Land Registry cannot provide scaled measurements from title plans or OS mapping.
Enlarging a map does not improve the accuracy of its original survey scale.
Copying, reducing or enlarging a plan is likely to distort its accuracy.
The guide groups large-scale OS mapping into four accuracy categories.
Relative accuracy measures local positional consistency between mapped and ground features.
Ordnance Survey describes absolute or positional accuracy separately from relative accuracy.
For 1:1250 mapping the guide gives a 95 percent relative-accuracy confidence limit below plus or minus 0.9 metres.
The listed-building specification was last updated on 7 August 2025.
Publishers must provide one listed-building dataset.
CSV is an accepted listed-building publication format.
GeoJSON is an accepted listed-building publication format.
GML is an accepted listed-building publication format.
GeoPackage is an accepted listed-building publication format.
The listed-building dataset may be uploaded at a single URL.
The listed-building dataset may be served through an OGC Web Feature Service.
The listed-building dataset may be served through an ArcGIS API.
Field names may use hyphens, underscores or spaces.
Uppercase field-name characters are normalised to lowercase.
The outline dataset requires at least one row for each listed building.
Each listed-building reference must be unique within the provider dataset.
Each listed-building reference must remain permanent across updates.
The Historic England register reference may be used as the provider reference.
The name field should match the name in the listed-buildings register.
Listed-building geometry is supplied as a polygon or multipolygon.
Curtilage should be included when it is available under Historic England guidance.
All polygon points must use the WGS84 coordinate reference system.
CSV geometry must be encoded as Well-Known Text.
The listed-building field stores the Historic England List Entry Number.
A delisted building requires an end-date in YYYY-MM-DD format.
Local-plan publication requires local-plan, boundary, document and timetable datasets.
CSV is an accepted local-plan publication format.
GeoJSON is an accepted local-plan publication format.
GML is an accepted local-plan publication format.
GeoPackage is an accepted local-plan publication format.
The local-plan datasets may be uploaded at one URL.
The local-plan datasets may be served through OGC WFS.
The local-plan datasets may be served through an ArcGIS API.
Local-plan field names may use hyphens, underscores or spaces.
Uppercase local-plan field-name characters are converted to lowercase.
A local plan sets a vision and framework for development of an area.
The service accepts incomplete local-plan records and supports later improvement.
Each local-plan reference must be unique within the provider dataset.
Each local-plan reference must remain permanent across updates.
The local-plan name field contains the official plan name.
The description field gives a brief description of the plan.
period-start-date records the beginning of the period covered by the plan.
period-end-date records the end of the period covered by the plan.
Year-only and year-month values are accepted when a full date is unavailable.
Each local-plan-boundary reference must be unique and permanent.
A local-plan boundary is represented by a polygon or multipolygon.
WGS84 is preferred for local-plan boundary coordinates, with transformation offered when necessary.
The live listed-building dataset reports 382,254 records.
The live listed-building dataset reports 2 data providers.
The listed-building collector last ran on 24 July 2026.
The live listed-building dataset is point-based and does not define the affected extent.
The live listed-building dataset is licensed under Open Government Licence version 3.0.
The live listed-building-outline dataset reports 124,897 outlines.
The live listed-building-outline dataset reports 96 providers.
The listed-building-outline collector last ran on 24 July 2026.
The outline dataset does not consistently show curtilage and is only an indicative guide.
The outline dataset is a work in progress without full England coverage.
The live local-plan-boundary dataset reports 364 boundaries.
The live local-plan-boundary dataset reports one provider.
The local-plan-boundary collector last ran on 27 July 2026.
The current local-plan-boundary records were created by MHCLG pending authoritative replacements.
The dataset is intended to identify which local plan applies to an area.
The 1 metre composite DTM covers approximately 99 percent of England.
The composite DTM has 1 metre spatial resolution.
The product is a raster elevation model.
The DTM is produced from the last or only laser return.
Surface objects are removed from the DSM to create terrain-only elevation.
The terrain model uses bespoke algorithms and manual editing.
The current composite was produced in 2022.
It combines Time Stamped archive and National LIDAR Programme surveys.
Where surveys repeat, the newest best-resolution data is used.
Resampled source data uses bilinear interpolation before merging.
The composite includes surveys from 6 June 2000 through 2 April 2022.
The Environment Agency WCS example uses version 2.0.1.
The official WCS guidance exposes a GetCapabilities request pattern.
WCS GeoTIFF NoData pixels use the numeric value -3.4028235e+38.
GeoTIFF stores a two-dimensional numeric array, so NoData is represented numerically.
GeoTIFF was selected as an open-standard and storage-efficient elevation format.
Esri shapefile is a non-topological format for feature geometry and attributes.
The .shx file stores the feature-geometry index.
The .sbn and .sbx files store optional spatial indexes.
Contour and tide-line features are supplied in line shapefile layers.
Spot heights are supplied in point shapefile layers.
Each contour shapefile supply includes a tile metadata XML file.
OS Terrain 50 XML metadata follows the GEMINI metadata standard.
Metadata is supplied for national products and on a per-tile basis.
The XML metadata includes comments explaining tag meanings.
Metadata identifies whether the data structure is grid or vector.
Metadata records the 10 kilometre National Grid tile reference.
The metadata topic category is the INSPIRE elevation theme.
The metadata identifies British National Grid as the coordinate reference system.
The Esri auxiliary XML contains minimum, maximum, mean and standard-deviation height statistics.
The same styling statistics are supplied for every tile to keep colour ramps consistent.
Default Esri styling can be disabled by removing or modifying the auxiliary XML.
OS Terrain 50 represents a terrain surface with protruding buildings and trees removed.
